newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia investors turn to bonds as equities fall.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia investors turn to bonds as equities fall.

text.p: The fall in the Tunisian equities market is encouraging investors to turn increasingly to bonds and bond investment funds, but stocks are set for a rebound, Tunisian financial analysts said on Thursday.
The Tunis Stock Exchange index lost 10 percent in 1996 and turnover fell 33 percent to 625 million dinars from 927 million dinars in 1995.
Partly in reaction, Tunis banks have set up four new bond funds in less than a month, doubling the previous number.
In 1996, assets of the previous four bond funds grew 56.50 percent to 313 million dinars ($325 million) from 200 million dinars in 1995, figures obtained by Reuters showed.
In contrast, assets of mixed bonds and equity funds plunged by 54.27 percent to 193 million dinars from 422 million dinars.
Returns from bond funds in 1996 ranged between 6.66 percent and 7.31 percent, in a year when inflation averaged 3.7 percent.
But six of the 11 mixed bond/equity funds lost money during the year. The SICAV-Amen fund fell 15.26 percent and Arabia-SICAV 7.93 percent, while the maximum gain was 6.39 percent for Sud-Sicav.

"The bond funds were more profitable than the mixed funds in 1996 because of the fall on the Tunis Stock Exchange. Investors lost interest in equities and are preferring safer fixed income," Nejib Hajri, Director General of Societe Financiere de Gestion, one of Tunisia's main broking houses, told Reuters.

Brokers said the market slumped because share prices had risen far too much in past years and also because of the progressive introduction, starting last October, of the computerised dealing system with its greater price transparency.

"More transparency made share prices more realistic. As a consequence, investors deserted the mixed funds and there were massive sales during the last four months," Jacques Lipka, managing director of the markets department at brokerage house Compagnie Generale d'Investissement told Reuters.
But analysts said bond funds would continue to be favourites only in the short term, and predicted that mixed funds would rebound by the end of the year along with the stock market.
"Some shares will continue to fall, but I am optimistic about the future of the Tunis bourse. I see it rebounding by January 1998," Lipka says.

"I don't see the bond funds growing further because of the fall of the monetary market rate, which was cut by one point in November and by one more point on the day-to-day market, so the return of bonds is likely to stand at around seven percent," Hajri said.
"There is much potential for mixed funds to grow when the introduction of listed firms on the computerised system is completed at the bourse," he added.

As a consequence of the fall of inflation to 3.7 percent in 1996 from 6.3 percent in 1995, the monetary market rate was cut by one percentage point to 7.8125 percent last November, and last month fell to 6.8125 percent on the interbank day-to-day market because of higher liquidity.
High liquidity is reflected in the increased volume of bank bids for treasury bills in the past three weeks, taking rates lower, to 7.25 percent for 13- and 26-week treasury bills.

As of Thursday, seven companies among the 31 listed on the Tunis exchange were still traded on the blackboard but were expected to join the other stocks on the computerised system within a few weeks. ($1.04 dinar)
